passage: Esther redrew the decoration plan for the school's Harvest Day for the sixth time on Tuesday. The ribbons had gone from gold to teal and back to gold, and the schedule now lived on five different sheets. Nkechi, in charge of tables, waited on the steps with the rest of the team for a task. "Is this final?" Nkechi asked. "Not yet," said Esther, rubbing her eyes. Week by week the team shrank: seven volunteers, then five, then three. On the day, the stage was beautifully draped, and only three people were left to serve two hundred guests. Nkechi kept the tables going and thought about all those hours, and how little the guests noticed the ribbons.

qa.q: How many times did Esther redraw the decoration plan?
qa.a: Esther redrew it for the sixth time.

qa.q: What is Nkechi feeling while waiting on the steps?
qa.a: Nkechi feels frustrated and restless, waiting for a task while the plan keeps changing.

qa.q: What could Esther do instead of redrawing again, and why?
qa.a: Esther could fix the plan, give each volunteer a task and a date, and stop polishing, because the extra changes add little while the team's energy drains.

qa.q: How might the other volunteers see Esther's changes?
qa.a: They probably feel worn out and unneeded, since they wait for tasks that never settle, which is why the team shrank from seven to three.

grounding: The head organiser redesigns the decoration plan six times and rewrites schedules, wearing out the team, and the polish adds little while volunteers lose interest before the day.

passage:
Three days before the school's Teachers' Day celebration, the student council room smelled of glue and cold samosas.

"Version seven," Siddharth announced, holding up a new sketch of the stage backdrop. "I moved the flowers to the left. It balances better."

Hansa stared at the six older sketches pinned behind him. "Sid, the paper for version five is already cut."

"Then we cut again. And I've redone the schedule so the welcome speech is forty seconds shorter."

Two volunteers exchanged a look and quietly packed their bags. "We'll come tomorrow," one muttered. They didn't.

By the morning of the event, Hansa and Siddharth were gluing flowers alone. The teachers smiled politely at the backdrop. Nobody noticed which side the flowers were on. Hansa noticed only how empty the room had been.

qa.q: How many older sketches were pinned behind Siddharth?
qa.a: Six older sketches were pinned behind him.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt by the morning of the event?
qa.a: Hansa likely felt tired, lonely and let down, noticing mostly how empty the room had been after the volunteers left.

qa.q: What would you change first in Siddharth's approach?
qa.a: Fix the design after one round of feedback and put the saved time into giving volunteers clear, small jobs, since the extra polish added little.

qa.q: How did the constant changes look to the two volunteers?
qa.a: To them the work probably felt pointless and endless, since cut paper kept being wasted, so they drifted away and did not come back.

grounding: Shows a head organiser redesigning a plan many times and rewriting schedules until the team wears out and the polish adds little.

passage:
Dear Vasudha,

I owe you an apology, and a confession about the Children's Day fair.

You were right. I redid the stall layout six times. Every night I rewrote the timetable, then sent it to all nine volunteers at 11 pm with "small changes!!" By the second week, only four people were replying. By the final week, two.

On the day, the stalls looked fine. Honestly, version two looked fine too. No child cared about the exact angle of the ring-toss booth. What they cared about was that there weren't enough people to run the games, and the queues were long.

I think I was scared that if anything went wrong it would be my fault. So I kept polishing instead of letting it be done.

Can we get chai this week? I'll listen this time.

Ritu

qa.q: How many volunteers were replying by the final week?
qa.a: By the final week, only two were replying.

qa.q: Why did Ritu keep redesigning, and what feeling sat underneath it?
qa.a: Ritu admits feeling scared that anything going wrong would be Ritu's fault, so the anxiety showed up as endless polishing.

qa.q: What approach might have suited Ritu better?
qa.a: Agreeing on a good-enough layout early and a fixed date to stop changes would have kept volunteers' energy for running the games.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Vasudha may feel vindicated but also touched, since Ritu admits the mistake openly and asks to meet and listen.

grounding: A letter admits that repeatedly redesigning a layout and rewriting schedules wore out volunteers while adding little for the day itself.
